result.summary: Pausanias traces the Agiad kings of Sparta from Agis to Alcamenes. Under them Sparta joins colonies, expels the Cynurians, fights Argos, and destroys Ægys, Amyclæ, Pharis, Geranthræ and Helos. Lycurgus gives Sparta its laws.

scenes.title: Agis and the colonies
scenes.summary: In Agis's reign the Lacedæmonians join the colony of Patræ and the fleet of Grais, who settles Æolis.

scenes.title: Cynurians expelled; war with Argos
scenes.summary: Under Echestratus the Cynurians are expelled. Under Labotas, with Lycurgus as regent, Sparta first fights Argos, with little result.
scenes.stakes: Spartan territory and neighbouring subjects, disputed with Argos.

scenes.title: Lycurgus and the laws
scenes.summary: Under Agesilaus Lycurgus legislates, from Crete or Delphi. Pausanias cites Homer on Minos.

scenes.title: Conquests under Archelaus to Alcamenes
scenes.summary: Sparta enslaves Ægys, destroys Amyclæ, Pharis and Geranthræ, and loses Teleclus to the Messenians. Under Alcamenes it settles Crete and destroys Helos.
scenes.stakes: Spartan expansion against Achæan towns; Teleclus is killed.

alias_notes.explanation: Herodotus's spelling of the king's name.
Descendants of Eurysthenes are named for Agis.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias quotes Homer on Minos, friend of Zeus, to support the divine origin of Cretan law.

analysis.text: The passage records Sparta's gradual rise through colonization, war and conquest, told through the line of kings.
Pausanias weighs rival traditions about Lycurgus's laws (Crete or Delphi) and cites Herodotus, showing his method of comparing sources.

fun_facts.text: Sparta had two royal houses at once, the Agiad and the Eurypontid, so Pausanias covers each line separately.

language_notes.text: Agidæ: the Agiad house, one of Sparta's two royal families, named from Agis; the other line was the Eurypontidæ.
"In their prime" means those of fighting age; Cynuria was the borderland between Laconia and Argolis.
Herodotus (Book 1) mentions Lycurgus when discussing Sparta's laws in connection with Crœsus's inquiry about the Greeks; the spelling Leobotes is Herodotus's.
"_viz._" is an abbreviation of Latin videlicet, meaning "namely".
Quoted from Homer's Odyssey (Book 19); "bosom-friend" renders a phrase usually taken to mean Minos conversed with Zeus, hence divine help with laws.
Eurypontidæ: the second Spartan royal house, descended from Eurypon, which ruled jointly with the Agiadæ.
"No small feather in their cap" is an idiom for a notable achievement, here the translator's colloquial rendering.
Limnæ: a border town where a Spartan sanctuary of Artemis stood.

context_notes.text: Patræ became a leading city of Achaia on the northern Peloponnese coast; colonizing stories like this link Sparta to wider Greek settlement.
Penthilus was a son of Orestes; Æolis and Lesbos were settled by Greeks from the mainland, according to Greek tradition.
Lycurgus is the traditional author of Sparta's constitution and way of life; ancient writers disagreed on his date and sources.
Amyclæ lay close to Sparta and was later absorbed into it; it remained famous for its shrine of Apollo.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias cites Homer as authority, using poetry as evidence for Minos's divine link to Zeus and so for Cretan claims.
Pausanias directs the reader forward, presenting himself as an organizing guide who defers topics to their proper place.
The quick surrender of two towns is set against Amyclæ's long resistance, which magnifies the Dorians' eventual achievement.
